items.question: What made you decide to switch from business and finance to AI research?
items.object: Artificial intelligence as a reason to change academic focus

items.question: What made OpenAI’s o1 release exciting to you as a research direction?
items.object: OpenAI’s o1 release as a research motivation
items.answer: Interestingly, it was right at the start of the PhD that they announced o1, so it felt like the perfect thing to jump on and do research on this topic. I think there were two things that we were really excited about with the o1 release. The first one was the really strong reasoning performance that they showed on math tasks, but also science questions. The second really exciting one was that those gains seem to get better with more compute at test time, or test-time scaling.

items.question: How do you think sequential test-time scaling compares with parallel test-time scaling?
items.object: Parallel versus sequential test-time scaling
items.answer: At a high level, I see two different approaches to test-time scaling. One is you scale in parallel, and the other is you scale sequentially. In parallel means that you're running multiple computations independently. For example, you take one model and run the question through it multiple times, and then you aggregate those answers somehow. The most common way to aggregate them is majority voting, where you just take the majority answer. Similar to classical ensemble techniques in machine learning, this will slightly improve the performance of the model because you're not bound to one-off errors or mishaps of the model. You can do fancier things there, like have a reward model decide which output to pick. On the sequential side, you have the model generate a single reasoning trace, or reason in a single chain, and then iteratively refine what it's doing and improve on its previous current answer. Intuitively, I think this one should scale better because you're not making potentially the same mistake multiple times in parallel, but the model is reasoning in one continuous chain, so it can build on intermediate steps and try to arrive at a better answer.

items.question: How do you interpret the low training cost reported for S1?
items.object: S1's training cost and reproducibility
items.answer: On the cost front, our final training run took 26 minutes on 16 H100s. If you rent 16 H100s on one online platform—I looked at Prime Intellect, for example—it costs around, I think, $40 per hour, so that would be $20 for 26 minutes. Very cheap for that final run. Of course, we also use resources to generate the data and create other parts, but for the final training run, that's all you need. Since we published all of our datasets, anyone should be able to replicate our results with those 26 minutes of 16 H100s.

items.question: How did you decide which problems belonged in the s1 training dataset?
items.object: Problem selection for the s1 training dataset
items.answer: Initially, we collected some of the hardest questions we could find online. We took some really hard Olympiad questions covering subjects like math, physics, and others, but also brain teasers from quant interviews and these kinds of difficult problems where you think that a lot of reasoning is necessary. We assembled 59,000 of those, and then we went through a process to filter them down to just 1,000. The key criteria in this process were focusing on quality, diversity, and that they are very difficult. The way we quantified these three metrics is, for difficulty, we looked whether previous models could solve them. If they can't, then we thought these would be very challenging. Ideally, a previous poor model cannot solve them, but we still know that they are solvable, either by a really strong model being able to solve them or some indication that there's a solution or something like that.

items.question: How did you think about applying LIMA’s “Less Is More for Alignment” idea to your choice of 1,000 reasoning training examples?
items.object: LIMA (“Less Is More for Alignment”) and the choice of 1,000 reasoning training examples
items.answer: There's a great prior paper called LIMA, “Less Is More for Alignment.” In that paper they showed that with just 1,000 samples they were able to train a model that was a pretty good chatbot. Based off of the original Llama models, they used these 1,000 samples to fine-tune, and they framed this as the superficial alignment hypothesis, which is that to align a model you actually don't need that much data; you can make it much simpler. We wanted to revive that, but for reasoning, and that's where the 1,000 number came from. It's also somewhat catchy if we can do 1,000.

items.question: How do you compare Gemini Flash Thinking and R1 as sources of reasoning traces for training your models?
items.object: Gemini Flash Thinking and R1 reasoning traces as training data
items.answer: Initially we used the Google Gemini Flash Thinking API, and we just ran it over even the entire 59,000 questions. Then we took from the API the thinking trace and the solution. At that point in time they already had a reasoning model, and we directly took the traces and answers from that model. Later, after R1 was released, we switched to the R1 reasoning traces and found that they're much better. We were able to train a slightly better model with that that we just released recently, called S1.1.

items.question: How do you think the teacher model’s capability limits what you can achieve through distillation?
items.object: Teacher capability as a bottleneck in reasoning-model distillation
items.answer: I think one hypothesis is that you're bottlenecked by the capability of your teacher. In our case, for Gemini on one of the benchmarks, AIME, it got 60%, and after distillation we got 57 with our model. We decided to stop there because it felt like there's not that much room to go further if we keep distilling from Gemini. We're already very close to its performance, and we're just using its thinking traces and its answers, so how much further are we able to go? But then with R1, which had much better performance than Gemini, we went a lot further and performance improved. I think that is an important thing to think about: how good is your teacher? Ideally, of course, it's as good as possible. But that's not to say that you can't be better; maybe it is possible to get better than the teacher you're distilling from, but with 1,000 samples that's especially difficult.

items.question: How do you think a reasoning model’s use of test-time compute should relate to question difficulty?
items.object: Test-time scaling in reasoning models
items.answer: We run the model on those math benchmarks, but it always uses the same compute. Say we ask it, “What is 10 plus 10?” No matter what we do in the simple setup, it just always does a forward pass through the model and then provides an answer. There was no clear way at the time for us to change the test-time compute: how much time does it spend to think about this answer and reason through the question? For very hard questions, intuitively we'd like the model to think for longer because they are harder; it should take more time. For simple questions we don't want it to spend that much test-time compute, so it should give us an answer very quickly. Can we produce a plot that shows that if we provide the model with more of this test-time compute, its performance improves continuously?

items.question: How did you approach controlling how long a model reasons with budget forcing?
items.object: Budget forcing for controlling a model’s test-time compute
items.answer: The way we went about it is, again, trying to find a very simple approach. The one we put forth is called budget forcing. The idea is we have some test-time compute budget, and we usually measure that in tokens, which is how many text units the model produces. Given this budget, we just force the model to generate that long of a reasoning trace. Either we cut it off, so after it has generated, say, a thousand tokens, we just cut off the thinking, and then the model will be forced to provide its current best guess, current best answer. That works well for cutting it short, but the key question for us was, how do we extrapolate it? How do we make the model think longer when it wants to stop and provide its current answer? For that, we force the model to continue thinking by injecting “wait” into its current reasoning trace.

items.question: Why do you think injecting the word “wait” into a model’s reasoning trace can improve its answer?
items.object: Injecting the word “wait” into a model’s reasoning trace
items.answer: When the model is currently generating its answer to some question, it might be something like, “Okay, given what I've reasoned above, the final answer should be three,” and then it wants to finish and stop the generation. What we do is disallow that and just put “wait,” and then let the model continue reasoning through it and generate further. What the model will do is be like, “Wait, is this correct? Let me go through it once more.” The way we train these models is through next-token prediction, where they learn to predict future words. If we provide the word “wait,” then the future word after that is most likely something like, “Wait, is this correct? Wait, let me do this once more.” We have some of these “wait” examples even in the 1,000 samples; some of the reasoning traces are naturally something like, “Wait, let me recheck this.” The model learns to generate these tokens after “wait,” and then, when it rechecks, it goes through it once more. If the previous answer was incorrect, then it is likely that it will change it and improve on its answer to get a correct answer. If it is already at a correct answer, you might think, “Okay, might this impair the model and lead it to an incorrect answer?” While this can happen, it's generally less likely. It might do something like, “Wait, let me double-check this,” and then it'll be like, “It seems my original answer was correct.” We think it's less likely because verification is easier than solving. When the model verifies its current answer, then it's easier for the model to know whether or not it's already correct.

items.question: Why do you expect injecting “wait” during inference to make the model continue reasoning?
items.object: Injecting “wait” to extend a model's reasoning during inference
items.answer: We do it in the inference loop generation. Specifically, we set the end-of-thinking token. The way our generation works is that we put in a question, and then after the question there's a delimiter that denotes the beginning of the reasoning process or thinking process, and then there's an end token, or end-of-thinking token, after which the model will generate its final answer based on its thinking process. Whenever the model tries to generate this end-of-thinking token delimiter, we disallow that. We have it as a stop token in our generation pipeline, and then instead inject “wait” right into the model's current generation. Then it'll just continue generating off from there. After “wait,” it's very unlikely that the model will just try to put the end-of-thinking token again because now a new sentence started. It'll do some more thinking and reasoning and hopefully get a better answer.

items.question: How do you think about the limit on how many times you can insert “wait” to extend a reasoning model’s thinking?
items.object: The number of “wait” insertions used to extend a reasoning model’s thinking
items.answer: We always pick the same number and found in our experiments that up to four can lead to performance gains, but beyond four times eventually the model will go crazy because it's getting “wait” all the time, and then it'll just go off into an infinite loop and bad things happen. Up to four times it's still relatively natural and the model will probably use them to improve its performance, so we got pretty consistent math gains up to that degree.

items.question: How do you think about combining “wait” prompts with token budgets to improve a reasoning model’s performance at test time?
items.object: Budget forcing with “wait” and token limits for test-time scaling
items.answer: We can combine it with a maximum, or we could also set a minimum token budget for the thinking trace, but generally we find just adding “wait” is enough to get us some additional test-time compute with better performance. Varying that a lot doesn't bring further gains. To tie back to budget forcing and cutting off the generation, if we put these together, then what we arrive at is a plot where we have different test-time compute budgets—say, we cut off at 1,000 tokens, 2,000 tokens, 3,000 tokens—and then we force “wait” one time, force “wait” two times, three times, four times. Each of those dots has better performance, and we get a very clean test-time scaling trend.

items.question: How do you think about setting a test-time compute budget for a reasoning model when its thinking length already varies by question?
items.object: Setting test-time compute budgets for reasoning models
items.answer: The idea is that ahead of time you have an idea of how expensive your question is to the model or how much you want the model to think about it, and based on that you set your test-time compute budget constraints for the model and then let it go with that. You could make it variable as well, so having the model itself decide, but that's kind of already happening in the original thinking trace. Naturally, the model will use different amounts of tokens for different questions, so we already have that. If I additionally want to set a budget constraint to enforce something, I might say the model should answer in one minute or ten minutes.

items.question: Why do you see data decontamination as important when evaluating large language models?
items.object: Data decontamination in large language model training
items.answer: One big problem in large language model training is that we're training these models on huge amounts of data, and when we evaluate them there's a chance that some of that evaluation data was in the training data. Then the evaluation isn't really proper anymore because the model has seen these things already; it might just be reciting its training data and not generalizing or really improving performance. That's why we employ decontamination. In our case, what we do is we take all of the evaluation samples and check for any matches in our training data. If there's any match, then we discard the sample from our training data. Since we only have 1,000 samples, that's relatively easy to do, but for pretraining that's a pretty big problem: you need to decontaminate against trillions of tokens, which is a very expensive process.

items.question: What did you learn from using rejection sampling to study scaling across different reasoning-chain lengths?
items.object: Rejection sampling for studying scaling across reasoning-chain lengths
items.answer: One very simple idea is to do rejection sampling. We thought that rather than having to have explicit control before we test the model, we just do it ad hoc after we've tested the model. We sample from the model multiple times, and naturally for the same question, if we sample from the model again and let it try to solve the question again, then it will solve it slightly differently, as long as there's some nondeterminism, which usually happens by having temperature sampling or something like that. This way we have a chain of a different length, and we do this multiple times, and then we sort them such that we get chains of different lengths for all the problems and look at how the scaling behaves. Surprisingly, what we found is that it's actually inverse.

items.question: How do you assess rejection sampling as a way to scale test-time compute?
items.object: Rejection sampling for scaling test-time compute
items.answer: It scales the exact opposite as we'd like it to: with more test-time compute, performance gets worse if we sample and rearrange this way. My hypothesis for why this is happening is that when we just try to choose the longest generations from the model, often these are the generations where the model was going off on a wrong track and backtracking multiple times and ultimately ending up with a completely wrong answer. The ones where it was correct maybe just jumped to the right answer right away, and that's why they're pretty short. So there's this inverse scaling trend for rejection sampling, and also it's not a very clean method because you can control it only after generating multiple times.

items.question: How do you assess the reproducibility of your s1 reasoning model given what you've released?
items.object: Reproducibility and open-source scope of the s1 reasoning model
items.answer: We've released everything, and there have been people that submitted issues and replicated parts of it. I haven't seen a full replication, but I'm pretty sure it should be possible. Everything is open source and the training only takes 26 minutes, so if you can afford the GPUs for those 26 minutes, which is roughly $20, then you should be able to do that. One part that we cannot open source is related to the base model because we didn't train that ourselves. We used the Qwen model from Alibaba, and we don't have the pretraining data for that one. Everything we do on top of that model, which is our paper, is fully open source.

items.question: Why do you see bias as a significant issue when using ChatGPT or Claude to evaluate models?

items.question: Why do you use OpenAI models to judge answer equivalence when your evaluation benchmarks already have ground-truth answers?
items.object: Using OpenAI models to judge answer equivalence in benchmark evaluations
items.answer: Yeah, our evals all had answers, but because the answers are very difficult to extract sometimes—for example, when the model generates a long math reasoning trace and then uses some formula to express its answer—it's very hard to just do a basic string match in Python. Rather, what we do is ask OpenAI models, maybe GPT-4, to tell us if these two answers are the same, and if yes, then we give it a go. We ask if the ground-truth solution we provided and the answer from our model are equivalent.

items.question: How do you think about supervised fine-tuning versus reinforcement learning as approaches to training reasoning models?
items.object: Supervised fine-tuning versus reinforcement learning for reasoning models
items.answer: For the RL versus SFT one, as you mentioned, R1 did RL, as OpenAI also claimed in their blog post, and we only did SFT. While we can get really good performance with SFT, there's some speculation that RL generalizes better. The intuition behind that is that RL incentivizes the model to arrive at a better answer regardless of its approach, versus for SFT we force it to follow a certain approach because we train it on the tokens themselves that lead to a certain answer, and that could even be an incorrect answer. Potentially, with more compute the RL approach might be better than the SFT approach. There's an interesting saying I heard from Hung-yi that might give some more nuance: “Give a man a fish, you feed him for a day; teach him how to fish, and you feed him for a lifetime.” Teaching him how to fish is a little bit like SFT.

items.question: How do you think about the role of the reward model in PPO training?
items.object: The reward model in PPO training
items.answer: With PPO, the way it works is that there's a separate reward model. The model generates something, and then that reward model will tell how good that generation is. We optimize based on that, so the model just gets a reward for its full text generation without forcing it to generate some text in particular. It can generate whatever it wants, but then it will be graded based on how good that generation is, and that's then back-propagated into the model as a signal, so it wants to maximize that reward. If the reward model is really good, so it grades text that leads to the right answer and has the right formatting or reasoning trace or whatever we want, then that should lead to a model that will be really good. But of course you can hack the reward model, which is often referred to as reward hacking. Maybe there's some way where the model will generate some really weird things, but nonetheless that leads to a really high reward because it exploits some weakness of the reward model. I think that's also why RL is generally a bit harder to get to work and sometimes very unstable.

items.question: How do you assess prompting a reasoning model with a token budget as a way to control how long it reasons?
items.object: Controlling a reasoning model’s token budget through prompting and supervised fine-tuning
items.answer: I think currently it is only the budget forcing for a final model, but we did experiment with other approaches. One very simple idea we had was, let's just tell the model in the prompt, “You've got 10,000 tokens. Go reason, figure it out.” But unfortunately the model doesn't really care what we tell it, and it'll just reason for much longer or do whatever it wants. We tried to SFT that in, so we trained the model on these kinds of prompts, and then the reasoning traces we trained it on would always adhere to that limit, but at inference it didn't care. Maybe it's just an issue of scale; maybe we need to have a better model in the first place. That would be a very intuitive way to do it.

items.question: What do you find most exciting about extending the test-time scaling you've demonstrated with s1?
items.object: Extending test-time scaling beyond repetitive loops and context-window limits
items.answer: What I'm really excited about is making the test-time scaling that we've shown cleaner and scaling further. Right now there's two key problems with it. One is that it does eventually flatten out. If you do “wait” too much, then eventually the model will just go into a repetitive loop and it won't get to the correct answer. How can we scale further when we want the model to think for not just minutes but for hours or days or a few years even, for really, really hard questions? The second part, which is kind of related, is that our model will run out of context window if it thinks for too long. These models have a fixed context window that they can operate on, and if they generate too much then it doesn't work anymore. At least for most models; some models have an architectural change that fixes that, but most models still have this limitation. We weren't able to scale beyond 32,000 tokens with sequential scaling, but we were able to use parallel scaling techniques like majority voting to scale further. We generate multiple times in parallel, and even though all of them reach 32K max together, they do a lot more than 32K, and then we aggregate them to hopefully arrive at a better answer. Solving these two issues is really exciting to me, so that we can use these models to solve some of our hardest questions, like curing cancer and so on.
